title: Lava and Kusha
hookLine: Valmiki takes Sita in, and teaches her twin sons to sing the Ramayana
carry: the ramayana lives by being sung
tomorrow: Sita goes home to the earth

lines: VALMIKI COMES DOWN TO THE WATER.
THE POET STEPS INTO THE STORY.
cards: Sita doesn't stay alone on the riverbank for long. Young hermits find her weeping and run to tell their teacher, and he comes down to the water himself.
It's Valmiki, the poet, the man who, at the very start of this serial, heard a bird's cry and found the first verse. He takes Sita by the hand and walks her to the women of the hermitage.
The poet of the story has just stepped into it.

teach.b: Valmiki tells Sita he knows she's done nothing wrong, and gives her a home among the hermit women. Months later, she gives birth to twins.
Valmiki prepares protective rites for the newborns with kusha grass, the sacred grass of Vedic ritual.

teach.h: KUSHA AND LAVA: NAMED FOR GRASS.
teach.b: The elder is touched with the tops of the grass, so he is Kusha; the younger with the lower part, the lava, so he is Lava. Then Valmiki folds the whole poem back on itself.

teach.h: THE SONS LEARN THEIR FATHER'S STORY.
teach.b: As the boys grow, he teaches them the Ramayana: this very song, with their father as its hero. They learn it by heart and sing it beautifully. Years later, Rama holds a great horse sacrifice, the ashvamedha.
Valmiki brings the boys, and they sing the poem in the open, day after day. Crowds gather. Rama hears it, is moved, and doesn't yet know whose sons are singing.
The poem's very first book opens with Kusha and Lava singing it before Rama, so the frame was this moment all along. Here's the teaching.

The Ramayana was made to be sung and heard, and Hindus still keep it that way: a grandmother singing over the stove, a Ram katha at the temple that runs for days, the Ramlila plays at Dussehra, a family reading a chapter aloud together.
Hearing sacred stories, shravana, is counted as a form of devotion in itself.

teach.h: A STORY MADE TO BE SUNG.
teach.b: And the first people to carry this one were two children who learned it by heart.

how: Lava and Kusha are familiar in temple paintings, folk plays and children's books; and Hindus still learn the Ramayana by ear, in temple kathas, Ramlila plays at Dussehra and songs at home.

o: the hermit boy who finds Sita weeping by the river
Sita's son, named for the tip of the sacred grass
the horse set free for Rama's great sacrifice

games.q: two boys in the hermitage — tap the pairs.
p: touched with the tops of the grass
hearing sacred stories, a form of devotion

s: Lava and Kusha are named for kusha grass used in their protective rites
the elder from the grass tops, the younger from the lower part, the lava.
Hindus count hearing sacred stories as devotion in itself
shravana, hearing, is the first of the Bhagavata's nine ways of bhakti.
Rama knows at once that the singers are his sons
he hears them and is moved, before he knows whose sons they are.

games.q: you want a child in your family to know the Ramayana. by Valmiki's own example, where do you start?
o: hand them the book and a quiz.
sing it with them until they know it by heart.
wait until they're old enough to read it in Sanskrit.
games.why: Valmiki taught Kusha and Lava by singing, and they carried the whole poem. Hindus still pass it on by voice: katha, Ramlila, a grandmother's songs.

practice: Many Hindus sing a simple line for Rama: Sri Ram, Jai Ram, Jai Jai Ram. Say it or sing it softly, slowly, for two minutes, and listen to your own voice the way the crowd listened to the twins.
If you don't pray, hum a song someone in your family taught you, and notice who you learned it from.

wordCard.voice: Kusha, Sita's son, named for the tip of the sacred grass used at his birth rite. With his twin Lava, he grows up in Valmiki's hermitage, learns his father's story, and sings it before him without knowing.

orig.note: Sanskrit kuśalavau: Kusha and Lava, the twins, named together in the dual form.

carryVoice: Your line: the Ramayana lives by being sung. Two boys carried it first. That's the week. Rest well.
